title: Five ways in which curriculums can get in the way of learning happening.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton lists five ways a curriculum can obstruct learning, treating curriculum as any set of documents used to plan it. It can be too full, because governments and subject enthusiasts keep adding to it, which pushes teachers toward coverage, exam guessing and memorised knowledge. It can be poorly written, for instance labelling knowledge outcomes as understanding. It can be unbalanced between knowledge, skills and understanding or among subjects. It can lack coherence when teachers pick activities from the internet. And it can waste teacher time when a school writes its own, as it did in his own acting headship. The post ends with a checklist and the lesson that adopting and adapting a proven curriculum usually serves students better.
points: An over-full curriculum turns coverage into the school's real priority and leaves too little time for the repeated experiences that learning requires.
Learning outcomes need precise wording, and understanding is often claimed for what is actually knowledge in disguise.
A curriculum can be unbalanced toward knowledge, toward skills, or by squeezing out arts and PE, each of which narrows learning.
Ad hoc internet activities lack coherence across classes and years, while school-written curricula typically consume teachers' limited time with little to show.
quotes: You might think that it is pretty obvious that a curriculum should be designed to fit into the time that is needed and available for learning to happen but many (most, in my view) curriculums just aren’t designed this way. Largely, this is because curriculums are often seen as dumping grounds for every issue that someone thinks matters, usually someone miles away from actual schools and classrooms.

A too full curriculum is like offering your help to someone for an hour or so and being given 12 things to do that will take at least 3 days to achieve. As my grandmother frequently used to say, ‘You can’t put a quart in a pint pot’.

In other words, an over full curriculum forces teachers to worry more about whether everything has been covered than whether real learning has taken place. Coverage becomes the Hedgehog Concept. Not learning.
Because we know the differences between knowledge, skills and understanding, we can see that the second outcome isn’t about understanding at all. It’s a knowledge learning outcome in disguise.

We had an unbalanced curriculum. Where were the skills of science, the hypothesising, the investigation design, the holding of variables, the careful accumulation of evidence, the weighing of our hypotheses against what actually happened and so on? They were non-existent.

Curriculums that are randomly grabbed by individual teachers from the internet are unlikely to be coherent and comprehensive. They can’t give a school confidence that what is being planned for children’s learning is appropriate in terms of activities or the timing of those activities.
Collectively, we didn’t have the experience, abilities or time we needed to write a curriculum. We really had bitten off more than we could chew.
